title: Chest pain in clinic: who goes to the emergency department, and what to do for the rest

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the 2021 AHA/ACC chest pain guideline and standard emergency practice. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: Which features of chest pain in clinic mean an ambulance to the emergency department rather than any office work-up?
a: Ongoing pain at rest for more than 20 minutes
d: Pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall
Pain that started a month ago and is unchanged
questions.why: New-onset or crescendo angina goes the same way even without these. The office is for stable, recurrent, exertional pain that has been the same for weeks.

questions.q: Within how many minutes of arrival should a patient with suspected acute coronary syndrome have a 12-lead ECG?
questions.why: ST elevation on that first ECG starts the reperfusion clock. It is repeated if the first is nondiagnostic and symptoms continue.

questions.a: Substernal discomfort, brought on by exertion or emotion, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin
d: Pain that lasts more than an hour
questions.why: All three features make it typical; two make it atypical; one or none makes it noncardiac. Women, older adults and people with diabetes more often present without the classic pattern.

questions.q: Which blood test, repeated over a few hours, rules myocardial infarction in or out?
questions.why: A single very low value drawn at least three hours from symptom onset rules out infarction in most pathways; otherwise a 0 and 1 to 3 hour pair does. A rise and fall makes the diagnosis.

questions.q: What dose of aspirin is given for suspected acute coronary syndrome?
questions.why: Chewing gets it absorbed within minutes. It is withheld only for true allergy or active bleeding.

questions.q: A patient with chest pain took sildenafil last night. What must be avoided?
questions.a: Nitroglycerin, for 24 hours after sildenafil and 48 hours after tadalafil
questions.why: The combination causes profound hypotension. Asking about erectile dysfunction drugs is part of every chest pain history, including from women, since the drugs are also used for pulmonary hypertension.

questions.q: Tearing chest pain radiating to the back, a pulse deficit, and a widened mediastinum. Which test?
questions.why: Aortic dissection kills at about 1% an hour untreated. Aspirin and anticoagulants are withheld until it is excluded, and blood pressure is brought down with a beta blocker.

questions.q: Sharp chest pain worse lying flat and better sitting forward, with a friction rub and diffuse ST elevation. What is the treatment?
questions.why: Colchicine roughly halves recurrence of pericarditis. Steroids are avoided as first line because they raise recurrence.

questions.q: A HEART score at or below what value identifies low-risk chest pain suitable for early discharge with a negative troponin?
questions.why: The score combines history, ECG, age, risk factors and troponin. A score of 4 to 6 means observation and further testing; 7 or more means early invasive evaluation.

questions.q: Stable chest pain, intermediate pretest probability, age 55, no known coronary disease. Which first test is reasonable?
questions.why: CT angiography excludes disease well in this group. Stress testing is the alternative, chosen when the patient can exercise and the ECG is interpretable, or when CT is impractical.

questions.q: Which drugs are standard for a patient with confirmed stable angina?
questions.why: A calcium channel blocker or long-acting nitrate is added if symptoms persist. Revascularisation is for refractory symptoms or high-risk anatomy, not for prognosis in most stable patients.

questions.q: Chest wall tenderness reproduces the patient's pain. What does that finding do to the probability of a coronary cause?
questions.why: Some patients with infarction have tender chest walls. Reproducible pain, pleuritic pain and positional pain each lower the likelihood, but the ECG and troponin still decide.
